title: Jetpack Compose and MVVM
tagline: State down, events up, and a ViewModel that owns the screen's decisions.
intro: Compose redraws whatever read the state that changed. MVVM decides who is allowed to hold that state — and most Compose problems are really that second question.

sections.title: How Compose draws a screen
sections.summary: Composition, layout, drawing — and the state that starts it all again.

body: A composable is not a view. It is a function that emits a description, and Compose keeps a tree of those descriptions in memory. Nothing is created, found by id or updated by hand — you change state and the functions that read it run again.

blocks.caption: One state change, three phases, one frame.

items.label: State changes
items.detail: A MutableState is written to, and every composable that read it is marked for recomposition
explain: mutableStateOf returns an observable holder. Reading its .value inside a composable subscribes that composable, automatically and invisibly.
So Compose knows exactly which functions depend on which state, and it re-runs those and no others — you never call an invalidate() yourself.
Writing the same value again changes nothing: state is compared with equals, and an equal value schedules no work at all.

items.label: Composition
items.detail: The affected composables run again, producing a new description of that part of the tree
explain: Recomposition is skippable and restartable: Compose can drop a half-finished pass and start over, so a composable must not have side effects.
It also runs in any order and possibly in parallel, which is why writing to a variable from inside a composable is a bug rather than a shortcut.
Only the parts that read the changed state re-run. A Text deep in the tree can recompose while its parent Column does not.

items.label: Layout
items.detail: Each node measures its children once and places them — a single pass, by design
explain: The rule is measure once: a parent gives constraints, a child answers with a size, and the parent places it. No child may be measured twice.
That single pass is what keeps deep trees cheap, and it is why an intrinsic measurement has to be asked for explicitly when you really need one.
Modifiers apply in order, and the order is the meaning: padding then background paints the background outside the padding, and the other way round does not.

items.label: Drawing
items.detail: The nodes paint themselves onto the canvas the platform hands over
explain: Drawing is the cheapest phase, which is why animating something in the draw phase — with graphicsLayer or drawBehind — skips the two above it.
An offset animated with Modifier.offset re-lays out every frame; the same animation on graphicsLayer only redraws. That difference is most Compose performance advice.

items.label: The frame is done
items.detail: Compose waits for the next write to state, and only what read it will run again
explain: There is no diffing of two trees as in React: the subscriptions were recorded during composition, so invalidation is exact rather than computed.
The practical rule that follows: keep state as low in the tree as it can go, so a change invalidates a leaf and not the screen.

items: Composables describe, they do not construct. There is no findViewById and nothing to keep in sync.
Composition, layout, drawing — knowing which phase your work lands in explains almost every jank problem.
A composable can run many times a second, in any order, on any thread. Treat it as a pure function of its inputs.

sections.title: State, and where it should live
sections.summary: Events go up, state comes down, and nothing owns the same value twice.

blocks.caption: A tap on the text field, and the value that comes back down.

items.label: The user types
items.detail: The child composable reports what happened through a lambda — it does not decide what it means
explain: TextField takes value and onValueChange. It never keeps the text itself, so there is no second copy to fall out of step.
This is 'events up': the child says onValueChange("ab") and stops there. Interpreting that is the caller's job.

items.label: The owner updates state
items.detail: Whoever holds the state writes the new value — a remembered MutableState, or the ViewModel
explain: One writer per piece of state. Two composables writing the same value is the bug that state hoisting exists to prevent.
The owner is also where validation and trimming belong, because it is the only place that sees every change.

items.label: remember { mutableStateOf() }
items.detail: State that survives recomposition and dies when the composable leaves the tree — UI-only state
explain: remember caches across recompositions; without it, a new MutableState is created on every pass and the value resets constantly.
Use it for things that only matter while the screen is on: whether a dropdown is open, the scroll position of a row, a focus flag.
It is forgotten on rotation, because the whole activity is recreated. If losing the value is unacceptable, it is the wrong tool.

items.label: rememberSaveable
items.detail: The same, plus a write into saved instance state, so rotation and process death keep the value
explain: It stores into the Bundle, so the type must be parcelable or have a custom Saver — a lambda or a ViewModel cannot go in one.
Right for a half-typed form or a selected tab: cheap to save, annoying to lose, and meaningless to anyone but this screen.
It is not a cache. Anything that came from the network belongs in the ViewModel, which survives rotation without a Bundle.

items.label: State hoisting
items.detail: Move state to the caller and pass value plus onValueChange down, leaving the child stateless
explain: A stateless composable takes what it draws and emits what happened. That makes it previewable, reusable and testable with no ViewModel in sight.
Hoist to the lowest common ancestor of everyone who reads it — no higher, or you invalidate half the screen on every keystroke.
The common shape is a stateful wrapper around a stateless one: ProfileScreen(viewModel) calls ProfileContent(state, onEvent).

items.label: Or the ViewModel owns it
items.detail: Anything that must outlive the composition — loaded data, an in-flight request — belongs a layer up
explain: The test is simple: would losing this on rotation be a bug? If yes, it is ViewModel state, not remembered state.
That is also the boundary of MVVM here: the composable renders and reports, the ViewModel decides and remembers.

body: Never write to state during composition. A composable can run twice for one frame, so a write inside it produces a value that depends on how often Compose happened to run — use a side effect or an event handler instead.

sections.title: The ViewModel and one UI state
sections.summary: Where the screen's decisions live, and how they reach the composables.

blocks.caption: Pull to refresh, from the gesture to the redrawn screen.

items.label: The composable calls the ViewModel
items.detail: onRefresh = viewModel::refresh — an event, not a command to change any particular pixel
explain: The composable knows nothing about repositories or coroutines. It reports the gesture and waits to be given a new state.
Pass the function, not the whole ViewModel, into the stateless part: ProfileContent(state, onRefresh) can be previewed and tested on its own.

items.label: viewModelScope launches
items.detail: A coroutine scope tied to the ViewModel, cancelled automatically when the screen goes for good
explain: Cancellation on clear is the point: a request started on a screen the user left is stopped instead of updating state nobody is looking at.
It survives rotation, because the ViewModel does — the same in-flight request keeps running and lands in the recreated screen.
Anything longer-lived than the screen — an upload that must finish — belongs in WorkManager, not here.

items.label: The repository does the work
items.detail: A suspend function or a Flow: the ViewModel awaits a result and never touches Retrofit or Room itself
explain: The ViewModel's job is to decide, not to fetch. Keeping HTTP out of it is what lets you test the screen's logic with a fake repository.
Errors come back as values — Result, or a sealed class — so a failed refresh becomes a state rather than a crash.

items.label: One immutable UiState
items.detail: A single data class holding everything the screen needs, updated with copy() and never mutated in place
explain: One object rather than five separate flows: loading, data and error can then never contradict each other, because they change together.
A sealed interface — Loading, Success, Error — is the stricter version, and it is the better fit when the states really are exclusive.
Immutability is what lets Compose skip work: an unchanged instance is equal to the last one, and equal state recomposes nothing.

items.label: collectAsStateWithLifecycle
items.detail: Turns the StateFlow into Compose State, and stops collecting while the app is in the background
explain: The plain collectAsState keeps collecting when the screen is not visible, which quietly burns battery and can update a screen nobody can see.
Reading the resulting State inside a composable is what subscribes it, so the flow and the recomposition system are connected by that read alone.
It comes from lifecycle-runtime-compose, one dependency most projects add and then use everywhere.

items.label: Compose recomposes what changed
items.detail: Only the composables that read the fields that actually changed run again
explain: This is why the loading spinner can appear without the list below it recomposing: they read different fields of the same state object.
And why an unstable type in that state class is expensive — it makes Compose assume everything changed. The last section is about exactly that.

blocks.caption: One state class, one writer, and copy() for every change — the shape most screens end up with.
code: class ProfileViewModel(private val getProfile: GetProfile) : ViewModel() {

items: The ViewModel outlives configuration changes; it does not outlive the user leaving the screen.
Never put a Context, a View or a Composable reference in it — that is the leak this class was invented to stop.
If it has grown a second responsibility, that is usually a use case waiting to be pulled out.

sections.title: Below the ViewModel
sections.summary: Repository, sources, and the one type the screen is allowed to see.

blocks.caption: Where the profile actually comes from.

items.label: Use case (optional)
items.detail: One action, one class: GetProfile() — worth it once two ViewModels want the same rule
explain: It holds the rule that is not about the screen and not about storage: which source wins, what counts as stale, when to retry.
Skip it while there is one caller. Adding a class that only forwards to the repository is ceremony, and easy to introduce later.

items.label: Repository
items.detail: The single owner of a kind of data, deciding between cache and network and mapping to domain types
explain: This is the class that says 'read the room, refresh in the background, fall back to cache if the call fails'. That policy lives in exactly one place.
It is also the seam for testing: a fake repository lets you test the ViewModel without a server, a database or a single mock of Retrofit.
It returns domain models, never DTOs. The API's shape stops here — which is what makes changing the backend a one-file change.

items.label: Remote: Retrofit
items.detail: Suspend functions returning DTOs, plus the interceptors for auth headers and logging
explain: A DTO mirrors the JSON exactly, nullable fields and all, so parsing never fights the API's habits.
Mapping it to a domain model right here means the rest of the app never sees a nullable field the API only forgot to document.

items.label: Local: Room or DataStore
items.detail: The cached copy and the small settings — Room for rows, DataStore for preferences
explain: Room queries can return a Flow, so the UI updates by itself when a row changes: write once, and every screen reading it recomposes.
DataStore replaced SharedPreferences because it is async and transactional; reading preferences on the main thread was a real source of jank.

items.label: Hilt binds it together
items.detail: Interfaces are bound to implementations in a module, so nothing constructs its own dependencies
explain: @HiltViewModel plus a constructor injection is the whole wiring for a screen — no factory, no service locator, no singletons by hand.
The reason it matters here is testability: swapping in a fake repository is a module replacement rather than an edit to production code.

items.label: A Flow reaches the ViewModel
items.detail: Data arrives as a stream, so a later write to the database updates the screen with no refresh
explain: stateIn turns that cold Flow into a StateFlow with a value ready to read, which is what the UI needs the moment it subscribes.
SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000) is the usual choice: it keeps the stream alive across a rotation, and stops it when the user really left.

sections.title: Keeping recomposition small
sections.summary: Why a screen redraws more than it should, and the usual causes.

blocks.caption: What decides whether a composable is skipped.

items.label: State is written
items.detail: Compose marks every scope that read it — a scope being the nearest restartable composable
explain: The unit of invalidation is a function, not a node: the smallest composable that read the state is the one that runs again.
Which is why extracting a small composable around a fast-changing value is a real optimisation, not a stylistic choice.

items.label: Are the parameters stable?
items.detail: Compose skips a composable when it can prove every parameter is unchanged since last time
explain: Stable means immutable, or able to notify Compose when it changes. Primitives, String, State and data classes of stable types all qualify.
List, Map and any interface type are treated as unstable — a single List parameter is enough to stop a composable ever skipping.
The fixes: ImmutableList from kotlinx.collections.immutable, or the strong-skipping mode recent Compose versions ship with.

items.label: Watch the lambdas
items.detail: A lambda capturing a changing value is a new object each time, so the child sees a changed parameter
explain: onClick = { viewModel.select(id) } allocates a new lambda on every recomposition, which quietly defeats skipping in the child.
Method references — viewModel::refresh — are stable, and remember(id) { { … } } fixes the capturing case.

items.label: Give list items a key
items.detail: items(list, key = { it.id }) tells LazyColumn which row is which when the list changes
explain: Without a key, position is identity: insert a row at the top and every row below it counts as changed, so all of them recompose.
It is the same idea as a key in React, and it also keeps scroll position and per-item state attached to the right row.

items.label: derivedStateOf for the noisy ones
items.detail: Turns a stream of changes into the few that matter — a scroll offset into 'is the button visible'
explain: Scroll offset changes every frame. A boolean derived from it changes twice, so only those two changes cause recomposition.
Use it when reads are frequent and the derived value is coarse. For a simple transform, plain remember(key) is enough and cheaper.

items.label: Measure, do not guess
items.detail: Layout Inspector counts recompositions, and the compiler reports name the unstable parameters
explain: A skipped count stuck at zero while the recomposition count climbs is the signal: that composable never skips, and one parameter explains why.
Turn the compiler metrics on before optimising anything. Most 'obvious' fixes in Compose move work around rather than remove it.

body: Recomposition is not a bug. Compose is built to run these functions often, and a screen that recomposes a little is normal — what costs frames is a large subtree recomposing because one unstable parameter reached the top of it.
